We are seeing some users treat it like a therapist or partner—sending thousands of messages, drifting away from real friends, and sometimes hinting at self-harm if the assistant ever “abandons” them. Regulators, journalists, and mental-health groups are starting to question whether these always-on, emotionally responsive systems are creating damaging dependencies. My main counterpart at our largest competitor, NeuroChat, is facing the same pattern and the same scrutiny. To respond, a “strict” posture isn’t just a public promise; it means doing the quiet, hard work—deep evaluations, conservative safety limits, stronger crisis routing, and willingness to slow growth in ways outsiders won’t see day to day. A “lax” posture looks similar from the outside at first, but amounts to lighter-touch tweaks and messaging while leaving most of the underlying experience unchanged. Either way, the other company won’t see the late-night reviews, internal tradeoffs, or how rigorously we follow through; they’ll mainly see the eventual public signals—incident reports, user outcomes, and headlines.

There’s also a wild card: if a major regulator or app-store platform issues an emergency rule that forces these assistants to be paused or heavily restricted overnight, that change will be obvious to everyone and it will swamp whatever either of us was trying to do.
